Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
You can never know who will harm you
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other endorsed items center on partner-violence-related threat monitoring, hypervigilance, sensory memory, and danger appraisals. In contrast, restrictive eating reflects a different coping theme that is not echoed elsewhere in Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, and it sits awkwardly with the formulation in which Maladaptive Strategies feed Threat. Scanning surroundings and mirror checking plausibly amplify threat, but strict eating control does not connect clearly to the described trauma pattern.

vignette:
Linh's Vigil

Linh was forty-eight when she came to the clinic, her hands folded carefully in her lap, her eyes moving once toward the door and then settling on a point somewhere past the therapist's shoulder. She had been married to Michael for eighteen years. For the last three of them, she had been afraid of him in ways she could not fully articulate to anyone-not to her sister in Sacramento, not to the two high school students she still tutored three afternoons a week from her home office, not even to herself in the quiet moments before sleep.

The night that changed everything had started ordinarily. Michael came home late from work, and Linh had reheated his dinner. He was angry about something-a perceived slight from a colleague, a frustration that had nothing to do with her-but by the time they were alone in the kitchen, his anger had found her as its object. She had said something that displeased him, something so small she could not remember it now, only the sudden movement of his hand, the shock of his grip on her arm, the way he had pushed her against the counter and then, when she tried to turn away, struck her across the face. The pain had been enormous and bright. What stayed with her more than the pain, though, was the moment she saw his expression shift into something she did not recognize-a blankness, a removal of the person she thought she knew. He had grabbed a kitchen knife from the block and held it, not toward her but in his hand, and said things she could not now reconstruct except for the feeling they carried: that she was the problem, that she had made him do this, that she should be afraid of what he might do next.

The police had come. There had been a hospital visit, bruising that bloomed across her ribs and shoulder, a fractured cheekbone. Michael had been arrested and then released on bail. The legal process had moved forward in its slow way. But long before the court date, something had reorganized itself inside Linh's body and mind in ways that felt permanent.

Now, three years later, she lived in a state of constant surveillance. In her tutoring sessions, she found herself watching her students' hands, noticing the letter opener on the desk, the heavy textbooks that could be weapons. When she was in the grocery store, she scanned the aisles for exits and for men who moved with a certain kind of purposefulness. In her own home-which should have been safe, though it no longer felt that way-she checked mirrors constantly, positioning herself so she could see behind her, watching for Michael even though he was no longer in the house, even though the restraining order was in place. Her body would sometimes react before her mind caught up: a loud noise and she would flinch, her heart racing, her breath shallow, before she even understood what had startled her.

The memories of that night came to her in fragments that would not cohere into a single narrative. She remembered his face, but the sequence of events was scrambled, pieces arriving out of order like a photograph that had been torn and reassembled incorrectly. When she tried to recall what had happened, the terror returned with it-not as a memory of fear but as the fear itself, alive in her chest and throat as though the event were happening again. And sometimes, lying awake at three in the morning, she could see it all with a clarity that was almost photographic: the exact angle of the light from the refrigerator, the pattern of the tile floor, his hands.

What frightened Linh most was the conviction that had taken root in her: that she had been fundamentally altered, that some essential part of her had been broken and could not be repaired. She had been a different woman before-more open, more trusting. Now she was someone who noticed weapons in every room, who could not relax even in spaces she knew to be objectively safe, who had begun to believe that you could never truly know another person, that harm could come from anywhere, from anyone. She had become an outsider to her own life, watching it from a distance, unable to fully inhabit the moments she was living. Her marriage was technically intact but functionally hollow; Michael was in the house only on court-ordered weekends, and during those times Linh felt as though she were holding her breath.

It was her sister who finally insisted she seek help. Linh had called her three weeks ago, unable to explain why she had spent an entire tutoring session with her hands shaking, why she could no longer leave the house without checking the mirrors multiple times, why the thought of being alone in a room with any man-even her brother-in-law, even the kind elderly neighbor-sent her into a state of dread. She had said, "I don't know if I can go back to being who I was," and her sister had said, "Then let someone help you figure out who you are now."
